patient.name: Terry Walsh
patient.setting: Emergency Department, then respiratory ward and clinic
patient.complaint: Four days of worsening breathlessness and green sputum
background: COPD diagnosed 4 years ago; salbutamol inhaler only
Two courses of antibiotics and steroids this year

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' in an older smoker with progressive exertional breathlessness, chronic productive cough and hyperinflation, and questions on the exacerbation organism (H. influenzae), the ABG and complications such as cor pulmonale.

points: Terry, 68, breathless for years; now **worse over 4 days**.
Cough with **green sputum**; more wheeze than usual.
Can only walk to the end of his front garden.

steps.lead: Terry's long-standing breathlessness is **persistent airflow limitation** from chronic bronchitis and emphysema.
Over 40, **50 pack-years** and building-site dust: his risk factors are textbook.

points: Barrel chest; using **accessory muscles**; pursed-lip breathing.
Prolonged expiration with **reduced breath sounds** and wheeze.
Central cyanosis; pitting oedema to mid-shin; JVP raised.

steps.lead: Worse breathlessness, purulent sputum and wheeze: an **infective exacerbation**, most often from **H. influenzae**.

steps.q: Which organism most commonly causes an infective exacerbation of COPD like Terry's?
steps.r: **H. influenzae** is the commonest bacterial cause. Pseudomonas appears in severe disease or bronchiectasis.

steps.title: Terry's ABG on air
steps.text: Low pO2, high pCO2, **raised bicarbonate** (chronic retention) but now a **low pH**: acute on chronic type 2 respiratory failure.

steps.lead: Terry's usual gas is **compensated** (normal pH, high CO2 and HCO3). Today the pH has fallen: his compensation is overwhelmed.
Terry's oedema, raised JVP and cyanosis suggest **cor pulmonale**; his ECG will show the right heart strain.

steps.text: Large **bullae** on a COPD X-ray can mimic a pneumothorax. Do not put a needle into a bulla: check for true pleural line and clinical signs first.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (spirometry: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7), CXR hyperinflation, ABG and ECG findings of right heart strain, and GOLD staging by FEV1 % predicted.

steps.q: Which test made Terry's diagnosis 4 years ago?
steps.r: **Spirometry**: a post-bronchodilator **FEV1/FVC below 0.7** confirms persistent obstruction.

steps.title: Terry's spirometry (post-bronchodilator)
steps.text: Obstructive, with **minimal reversibility**: COPD rather than asthma.

steps.lead: Terry's post-bronchodilator ratio of **0.42** confirms COPD.
Today's chest X-ray shows **flattened hemidiaphragms** and hyperlucent, hyperinflated lungs, with no consolidation or pneumothorax.
Terry is severe, so he has an **ABG**, and his ECG shows the **right heart** changes of long-standing hypoxia.

visual.title: Terry's 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: T inversion in V1-V3 (**RV strain**). The report adds tall P waves in II (**P pulmonale**) and **right axis deviation**.

visual.title: Terry's FEV1 (% predicted)
visual.label: Terry 42%
visual.caption: FEV1 **42%** predicted: **Stage 3 (severe)**, breathless on minimal exertion.

steps.q: Terry has 2 or more exacerbations a year and many symptoms. Which GOLD group is he?
steps.r: **2 or more exacerbations** with **more symptoms** = GOLD D. All from GOLD B upwards are offered pulmonary rehab.

steps.lead: Terry has **no asthmatic features** (no atopy, normal eosinophils, little reversibility), which guides his inhaler choice.

steps.text: Check **alpha-1 antitrypsin** in a young patient (under 45), a non-smoker, or with basal-predominant emphysema.

management.exam: Expect acute questions (controlled oxygen 88-92%, nebulised bronchodilators, prednisolone 5 days, amoxicillin, NIV for pH 7.25-7.35 with raised pCO2) and long-term ones (smoking cessation, LABA+LAMA vs LABA+ICS, LTOT criteria, azithromycin prophylaxis).

steps.q: Terry's SpO2 is 84% on air. Which oxygen should he get first?
steps.r: He is a **CO2 retainer**: give **controlled oxygen** via Venturi to **88-92%**. Never withhold oxygen.

visual.title: Oxygen target in COPD
visual.label: Terry 84% on air
visual.caption: Titrate the Venturi up until he sits in the **88-92%** band.

steps.lead: Terry gets nebulised **salbutamol and ipratropium**, **prednisolone 30 mg for 5 days** and **amoxicillin** for green sputum.

visual.title: Terry's gases
visual.caption: pH still **7.28** after an hour of medical therapy: start **NIV (BiPAP)**. It corrects within hours.

points: Five days later: off NIV, sats 90% on air.
Smoking cessation: **varenicline** and the stop-smoking service.
Home with a **rescue pack**: prednisolone and amoxicillin.

steps.lead: For Terry, **stopping smoking** improves survival more than any inhaler.
Breathless on salbutamol only, with no asthmatic features: Terry starts **LABA + LAMA**.

steps.title: COPD inhaler pathway
steps.caption: ICS raise **pneumonia** risk, so they need a reason: asthmatic features or exacerbations.

steps.lead: At 8 weeks, off cigarettes, Terry's stable PaO2 is **7.1 kPa** twice: he qualifies for **LTOT**, plus rehab and vaccines.

visual.title: Stable PaO2 and LTOT
bands: LTOT if oedema, polycythaemia, pulm HTN
visual.label: Terry 7.1
visual.caption: Below **7.3 kPa** on two stable gases: offer LTOT (only if not smoking).

steps.lead: Terry's CT shows **lower-lobe** emphysema and his PaCO2 is above 7, so he is not a candidate for lung volume reduction.
NICE NG115 and GOLD guided Terry's inhalers, LTOT and exacerbation plan.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanisms: protease-antiprotease imbalance from smoking, loss of elastic recoil causing gas trapping, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction causing cor pulmonale, renal compensation, and why oxygen is given cautiously.

steps.lead: Terry has both: **chronic bronchitis** (his sputum) and **emphysema** (his hyperinflation).

steps.title: Smoke to emphysema
steps.caption: Protease-antiprotease imbalance. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency does the same without smoke.

steps.lead: Fifty years of smoke kept Terry's **protease** load above his antiprotease defence.
With elastic recoil lost, Terry's small airways **collapse on expiration**, trapping air and flattening his diaphragms.

steps.q: Why has Terry developed ankle oedema and a raised JVP?
o: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction causing RV failure
steps.r: Chronic hypoxia constricts pulmonary arterioles, causing **pulmonary hypertension** and **RV failure** (cor pulmonale).

steps.lead: Terry's peripheral oedema is **cor pulmonale** from chronic hypoxia.
Terry's bicarbonate of 33 is the **kidneys** holding on to HCO3 over months to buffer his CO2.
Uncontrolled oxygen could have pushed Terry's CO2 higher, which is why he gets **88-92%**.

steps.text: Most CO2 rise with high-flow oxygen comes from worsening **V/Q mismatch** (loss of hypoxic vasoconstriction) and the **Haldane effect**, not only loss of hypoxic drive. The answer is the same: target 88-92%.

mcq.q: What is the most important risk factor for COPD?
Which organism most commonly causes an infective exacerbation of COPD?
What is the classic ABG of a stable CO2 retainer?
o: Low pH, high CO2, normal HCO3
Normal pH, high CO2, high HCO3
Normal pH, low CO2, low HCO3
High pH, low CO2, normal HCO3

mcq.q: Which ECG axis change is seen with RV hypertrophy in COPD?
An FEV1 of 40% predicted is which GOLD stage?
What is the oxygen saturation target in COPD with CO2 retention?
When is NIV indicated in an exacerbation?
mcq.r: **Respiratory acidosis** pH 7.25-7.35 with raised pCO2 despite medical therapy.

mcq.q: Which is the first maintenance step in breathless COPD without asthmatic features?

prompts.q: What is COPD and what are its risk factors?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: persistent, not reversible; smoker over 40.

points.p: Persistent airflow limitation
Emphysema and chronic bronchitis
Smoking is the most important risk factor
Age over 40, air pollution, occupational exposure
points.why: Check alpha-1 antitrypsin if young or non-smoker.

prompts.q: How does COPD present, and what are the signs?

points.p: Exertional dyspnoea and chronic productive cough
Prolonged expiration, wheeze, reduced breath sounds
Hyperinflation and accessory muscle use
Cyanosis and frequent infections

prompts.q: How does an infective exacerbation present, and which organism is commonest?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the green sputum question.

points.p: Worse breathlessness, cough with purulent sputum, wheeze
Haemophilus influenzae is commonest

prompts.q: What is the classic ABG in COPD, and what does a drowsy patient with high CO2 mean?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: look at pH and HCO3 together.

points.p: Compensated respiratory acidosis: normal pH, high CO2, high HCO3
Drowsy with high CO2 = type 2 respiratory failure, an emergency
Low pH with high CO2 and high HCO3 = acute on chronic

prompts.q: What complications of COPD must you know?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the right heart, the blood and the pleura.

points.p: Cor pulmonale (RV hypertrophy and failure)
Polycythaemia
Respiratory failure and infection
Pneumothorax (bullae can mimic it)

prompts.q: How is COPD diagnosed and what do the CXR and ECG show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: spirometry confirms; the rest support.

points.p: Spirometry: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7
CXR: flattened hemidiaphragms, hyperlucent, hyperinflated
ECG: P pulmonale, right axis deviation, RV strain
ABG if severe disease suspected

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: two systems, FEV1 stage and GOLD group.

points.p: Stage 1 FEV1 above 80%, Stage 2 50-80%
Stage 3 30-50%, Stage 4 below 30%
GOLD groups: 2 or more exacerbations a year = C or D; more symptoms = B or D
points.why: GOLD B and above get pulmonary rehab.

points.p: Asthmatic features: atopy, high eosinophils, FEV1 variation 400 mL, PEF variation 20%

prompts.q: How is an acute exacerbation of COPD managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: controlled oxygen first, then the NIV threshold.

points.p: Controlled oxygen, target 88-92% (Venturi)
Nebulised salbutamol with or without ipratropium
Oral prednisolone for 5 days
points.why: Plus a rescue pack at discharge.

points.p: Amoxicillin if purulent sputum (doxycycline or clarithromycin if allergic)
NIV (BiPAP) for pH 7.25-7.35 with raised pCO2

prompts.q: What is the long-term management of COPD?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the criteria for each intervention.

points.p: Smoking cessation: most effective for survival
SABA or SAMA, then LABA + LAMA (or LABA + ICS if asthmatic features), then triple
Pulmonary rehab and vaccines (annual flu, pneumococcal)
points.why: Rehab for GOLD B and above.

points.p: LTOT: PaO2 below 7.3, or 7.3-8 with oedema, polycythaemia or pulmonary hypertension
Azithromycin prophylaxis (ECG for QT, LFTs) and lung volume reduction surgery in selected patients

prompts.q: How does smoking cause emphysema and hyperinflation?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: protease versus antiprotease, then elastic recoil.

points.p: Smoke drives neutrophil and macrophage inflammation
Proteases (neutrophil elastase) overwhelm alpha-1 antitrypsin
Loss of elastic recoil: airways collapse on expiration, gas trapping

prompts.q: Why do cor pulmonale, compensated acidosis and oxygen sensitivity occur in COPD?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: hypoxia, kidneys and CO2.

points.p: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and remodelling cause pulmonary hypertension and RV hypertrophy
Kidneys reabsorb more bicarbonate to normalise pH
Reliance on hypoxic drive (and V/Q effects): high oxygen raises CO2, so target 88-92%

glossary.COPD: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: persistent airflow limitation from emphysema and chronic bronchitis.
glossary.Emphysema: Permanent destruction of alveolar walls with loss of elastic recoil.
glossary.Chronic bronchitis: Chronic airway inflammation with mucus hypersecretion and productive cough.
glossary.Pack-years: Packs of 20 cigarettes per day multiplied by years smoked.
glossary.Hyperinflation: Over-expanded lungs from trapped air: barrel chest and flat diaphragms.
glossary.Rhonchi: Low-pitched, snoring sounds from secretions in larger airways.
glossary.Cyanosis: Bluish skin or lips from low blood oxygen.
glossary.Spirometry: Breathing test measuring FEV1 and FVC.
glossary.FVC: Forced vital capacity: total air blown out after a full breath.
glossary.FEV1/FVC: Ratio of FEV1 to FVC; below 0.7 after bronchodilator confirms COPD.
glossary.DLCO: Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide; reduced in emphysema.
glossary.TLCO: Transfer factor for carbon monoxide; the UK term for DLCO.
glossary.GOLD: Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease: staging and grouping system for COPD.
glossary.Compensated respiratory acidosis: Raised CO2 with normal pH because the kidneys have raised bicarbonate.
glossary.Type 2 respiratory failure: Low pO2 with pCO2 above 6.0 kPa.
glossary.CO2 retainer: A patient with chronically raised CO2 who risks CO2 rise with uncontrolled oxygen.
glossary.Flapping tremor: Asterixis: a coarse flap of outstretched hands, seen with CO2 retention.
glossary.Cor pulmonale: Right heart failure caused by lung disease and pulmonary hypertension.
glossary.Pulmonary hypertension: Raised pressure in the pulmonary arteries.
glossary.P pulmonale: Tall peaked P waves (above 2.5 mm) in inferior leads from right atrial enlargement.
glossary.Right axis deviation: QRS axis beyond +90 degrees, often from right ventricular hypertrophy.
glossary.RV strain: ECG pattern of ST depression and T inversion in V1-V3 from right ventricular overload.
glossary.Multifocal atrial tachycardia: Irregular tachycardia with three or more P wave shapes, linked to COPD.
glossary.Polycythaemia: Raised haemoglobin and red cell mass, here from chronic hypoxia.
glossary.Bullae: Large air spaces in emphysematous lung that can mimic a pneumothorax.
glossary.Needle thoracocentesis: Needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax.
glossary.SABA: Short-acting beta-2 agonist, such as salbutamol.
glossary.SAMA: Short-acting muscarinic antagonist, such as ipratropium.
glossary.LABA: Long-acting beta-2 agonist, such as salmeterol or formoterol.
glossary.LAMA: Long-acting muscarinic antagonist, such as tiotropium.
glossary.ICS: Inhaled corticosteroid; raises pneumonia risk in COPD.
glossary.Venturi mask: Mask delivering a fixed oxygen percentage such as 24% or 28%.
glossary.NIV: Non-invasive ventilation through a tight mask, without intubation.
glossary.BiPAP: Bilevel positive airway pressure: the NIV mode used in hypercapnic COPD.
glossary.LTOT: Long-term oxygen therapy for at least 15 hours a day in chronic hypoxaemia.
glossary.Pulmonary rehabilitation: Supervised exercise and education programme for chronic lung disease.
glossary.Rescue pack: Prednisolone and antibiotics kept at home to start at the onset of an exacerbation.
glossary.Azithromycin prophylaxis: Long-term low-dose azithromycin to reduce exacerbations in selected patients.
glossary.Lung volume reduction surgery: Removing hyperinflated emphysematous lung to improve mechanics.
glossary.Alpha-1 antitrypsin: A liver-made antiprotease protecting alveoli from neutrophil elastase.
glossary.Neutrophil elastase: A protease from neutrophils that destroys alveolar elastin.
glossary.Elastic recoil: The lung's natural tendency to spring back, which drives expiration.
glossary.Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction: Constriction of pulmonary arterioles in response to low alveolar oxygen.
glossary.Hypoxic drive: Breathing stimulated by low oxygen rather than high CO2.
glossary.Haldane effect: Oxygen binding to haemoglobin releases CO2, raising blood CO2.
glossary.Haemophilus influenzae: Gram-negative coccobacillus; the commonest bacterial cause of COPD exacerbations.
glossary.Varenicline: A partial nicotinic agonist used to help people stop smoking.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man has a 3 year history of progressive breathlessness on exertion and a cough productive of white sputum every morning. He has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 45 years. He has no history of atopy. His chest is hyperinflated with a prolonged expiratory phase. His oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.

clues: productive of white sputum every morning
steps.x: Older heavy smoker, progressive exertional dyspnoea, chronic productive cough, hyperinflation, no atopy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **COPD**.

elim: Variable, episodic and often atopic; this is persistent and progressive.
Large volumes of purulent sputum daily and coarse crackles.
Orthopnoea, PND, oedema and basal crackles.
Dry cough, fine crackles, clubbing; restrictive, not hyperinflated.

steps.x: **C. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.** Rule: smoker over 40 + progressive dyspnoea + chronic sputum = COPD; confirm with spirometry.

technique.stem: A 59 year old woman who has smoked for 40 years has a 2 year history of exertional breathlessness and chronic cough. Her chest X-ray shows hyperinflated lung fields. Her GP wants to confirm the diagnosis.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show for this patient.
Suspected COPD; the question wants the confirming test.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Spirometry**: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7.

elim: Assesses severity and respiratory failure, not diagnosis.
The X-ray supports but cannot confirm COPD.
Shows emphysema but is not the diagnostic test.
Looks for cor pulmonale or heart failure, not obstruction.

steps.x: **E. Post-bronchodilator spirometry.** Rule: COPD is confirmed by spirometry, never by X-ray.

technique.stem: A 72 year old man with COPD has an infective exacerbation. After 1 hour of controlled oxygen, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, oral prednisolone and amoxicillin he remains breathless but alert. His pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 138/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% on 28% oxygen.
technique.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Increase oxygen to 15 L/min via non-rebreathe mask
Repeat nebulisers and review in 4 hours

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now.
Optimal medical therapy for an hour; persistent respiratory acidosis with a raised pCO2.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: pH 7.25-7.35 with raised pCO2: **NIV (BiPAP)**.

elim: Sats are on target; more oxygen will raise CO2 further.
For failure of NIV or if NIV is contraindicated; he is alert.
Rarely used, and does not treat ventilatory failure.
Persistent acidosis needs ventilatory support now.

steps.x: **D. Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP).** Rule: persistent respiratory acidosis after medical therapy = NIV.

technique.stem: A 70 year old woman with severe COPD has a 50 pack-year smoking history. CT shows widespread centrilobular emphysema. Her serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her alveolar destruction?
o: Autoimmune attack on type II pneumocytes

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to its mechanism.
Smoking-related emphysema with normal antiprotease levels.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Smoke recruits neutrophils and macrophages, whose **proteases** overwhelm antiprotease defences.

elim: Not the mechanism of emphysema.
This is fibrosis, the opposite of emphysema.
This is asthma.
Seen in sarcoidosis or berylliosis.

steps.x: **E. Neutrophil elastase overwhelming antiprotease defences.** Rule: emphysema = protease-antiprotease imbalance.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has slowly progressive breathlessness for 6 years and a cough with sputum most days. He worked in a shipyard 40 years ago and has a 45 pack-year smoking history. His chest is hyperinflated. His pulse rate is 92 bpm, BP 138/84 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows flattened hemidiaphragms and hyperlucent lung fields.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Progressive breathlessness, chronic sputum, hyperinflation and flattened hemidiaphragms in a heavy smoker are COPD. Asbestosis is restrictive fibrosis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.
Heavy smoker, progressive dyspnoea, chronic sputum, hyperinflation. The shipyard is a distractor.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **COPD**.

elim: A restrictive fibrosis with basal crackles and clubbing, not hyperinflation.
Episodic and variable; this is slowly progressive in a heavy smoker.
Chest pain, weight loss and a pleural effusion or mass.
Small lungs with reticular shadowing, not flattened diaphragms.

steps.x: **C. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.** Hyperinflation + flattened diaphragms in a smoker = COPD, whatever the asbestos history.

practice.stem: A 67 year old woman with COPD has 3 days of increased breathlessness and a change in sputum from white to green. She has no recent hospital admissions. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows no consolidation.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Haemophilus influenzae is the most common bacterial cause of an infective exacerbation of COPD; Pseudomonas suggests severe disease or recent hospital care.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.
Infective exacerbation of COPD without pneumonia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The commonest organism: **Haemophilus influenzae**.

elim: Upper lobe pneumonia in alcohol excess; there is no consolidation.
Pneumonia with hyponatraemia after water-system exposure.
Seen in very severe COPD, bronchiectasis or recent hospital stays.
Cavitating pneumonia, often after influenza.

steps.x: **A. Haemophilus influenzae.** COPD exacerbation organism = H. influenzae.

practice.stem: A 71 year old man with severe COPD attends clinic for review. He is at his usual level of breathlessness and has not had an exacerbation for 3 months. His respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. An arterial blood gas is taken.
practice.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of his arterial blood gas?
practice.e: Normal pH with raised pCO2 and raised bicarbonate is a compensated respiratory acidosis: chronic hypoventilation with renal compensation.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.

clues: not had an exacerbation for 3 months
steps.x: Stable severe COPD: normal pH, high pCO2, high HCO3.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chronic CO2 retention with renal compensation: **compensated respiratory acidosis**.

elim: The pH would be low and HCO3 normal.
Would need low HCO3 and low pCO2.
pH is normal and the primary problem is the raised CO2.
Needs a low pCO2.

steps.x: **B. Compensated respiratory acidosis.** Stable COPD gas = normal pH, high CO2, high HCO3.

practice.stem: A 74 year old woman with long-standing COPD has 2 months of worsening ankle swelling. There is pitting oedema to the knees, a raised JVP, a loud P2 and a left parasternal heave. Her chest is hyperinflated. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 86% breathing air.
practice.q: Which complication has she most likely developed?
practice.e: Chronic hypoxia causes pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular failure (cor pulmonale): oedema, raised JVP, loud P2 and a parasternal heave. Polycythaemia is also typical.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.
Chronic hypoxia plus right heart signs: oedema, raised JVP, loud P2 (pulmonary hypertension), RV heave.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Right heart failure secondary to lung disease: **cor pulmonale**.

elim: Needs a cause (TB, surgery) and shows Kussmaul's sign, not a loud P2.
Gives orthopnoea and basal crackles; signs here are right-sided.
Oedema with heavy proteinuria; no raised JVP or loud P2.
Rare, usually rheumatic; does not explain the parasternal heave.

steps.x: **B. Cor pulmonale.** COPD + right heart failure signs = cor pulmonale.

practice.stem: A 69 year old man with severe COPD and chronic hypoxia attends clinic. He has a 55 pack-year smoking history and mild ankle oedema. His pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 87% breathing air. An ECG is recorded. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: Terry's 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: T inversion in V1-V3 (**RV strain**). The report adds tall P waves in II (**P pulmonale**) and **right axis deviation**.

practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on his ECG?
o: Left axis deviation with left bundle branch block
P pulmonale with right axis deviation
Short PR interval with delta waves
Small QRS complexes with electrical alternans
practice.e: Chronic hypoxia causes RV hypertrophy and right atrial enlargement: P pulmonale, right axis deviation and an RV strain pattern. Low-voltage QRS can also occur from hyperinflation.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.
Long-standing hypoxia strains the right heart.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Right atrial enlargement (**P pulmonale**) and RV hypertrophy (**right axis deviation**).

elim: Suggests left-sided heart disease.
An anterior STEMI.
Wolff-Parkinson-White.
Classic of a large pericardial effusion.

steps.x: **B. P pulmonale with right axis deviation.** COPD ECG = P pulmonale, right axis, RV strain.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman with COPD is brought in by her daughter because she has become drowsy over the day. She was given high-flow oxygen by the ambulance crew. She has a flapping tremor and warm peripheries. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm, BP 150/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 12 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% on 15 L/min oxygen.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her drowsiness?
practice.e: A drowsy COPD patient with a high CO2 after uncontrolled oxygen has type 2 respiratory failure. Reduce oxygen to target 88-92% and consider NIV.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.
COPD, high-flow oxygen, drowsy with CO2 retention signs (flap, warm peripheries, bounding pulse).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Drowsy COPD patient with high CO2: **type 2 respiratory failure**, an emergency.

elim: Would give sweating and cool peripheries; no reason given.
No sodium result or cause given; does not explain the CO2 signs.
Pinpoint pupils and no opioid history.
No focal neurological deficit.

steps.x: **E. Type 2 respiratory failure.** Drowsy + COPD + high oxygen = CO2 narcosis.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man who smokes has breathlessness on exertion and a morning cough. He has no atopy. His GP suspects COPD and arranges a test to confirm the diagnosis. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
o: FEV1 rise of 18% after salbutamol with normal ratio
practice.e: COPD is confirmed by a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7. Marked reversibility or raised FeNO points to asthma.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show for this patient.
The confirming spirometry criterion for COPD.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Post-bronchodilator **FEV1/FVC below 0.7**.

elim: Marked reversibility suggests asthma.
A restrictive pattern.
Reduced in emphysema; normal does not confirm COPD.
Points to eosinophilic asthma.

steps.x: **D. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.58.** COPD = post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.7.

practice.stem: A 65 year old woman has COPD confirmed on spirometry. Her post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is 0.52 and her FEV1 is 38% of predicted. She is breathless on minimal exertion such as dressing.
practice.q: Which is her GOLD spirometric stage?
practice.e: FEV1 30-50% predicted is GOLD stage 3 (severe), with breathlessness on minimal exertion.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show for this patient.
Confirmed COPD; place the FEV1 % predicted.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: FEV1 **30-50%** = **Stage 3, severe**.

elim: Stage 1 is FEV1 above 80%.
Stage 2 is 50-80%.
Stage 4 is below 30%.
A ratio of 0.52 confirms obstruction.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man with COPD uses salbutamol as needed and remains breathless on exertion. He has stopped smoking and completed pulmonary rehabilitation. He has no history of asthma or atopy and a normal eosinophil count. His pulse rate is 78 bpm, BP 134/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: With persistent breathlessness and no asthmatic or steroid-responsive features, NICE advises LABA + LAMA. LABA + ICS is for asthmatic features.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now.

clues: no history of asthma or atopy
steps.x: Persistent breathlessness on SABA, no asthmatic features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dual long-acting bronchodilator: **LABA + LAMA**.

elim: Never ICS monotherapy in COPD.
Chosen when there are asthmatic or steroid-responsive features.
Needs a stable PaO2 below 7.3 kPa; his sats are 95%.
For exacerbations only, not maintenance.

steps.x: **C. LABA + LAMA.** No asthmatic features = LABA + LAMA; asthmatic features = LABA + ICS.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman with severe COPD stopped smoking a year ago. On two arterial blood gases 3 weeks apart, while clinically stable, her PaO2 is 7.0 kPa and 7.1 kPa breathing air. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 130/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 87% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: LTOT is offered when stable PaO2 is below 7.3 kPa (or 7.3-8 kPa with oedema, polycythaemia or pulmonary hypertension) in a non-smoker.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now.
Stable PaO2 below 7.3 kPa twice, non-smoker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Offer **LTOT**, delivered for 15 or more hours a day, target 88-92%.

elim: For exercise desaturation, not resting hypoxaemia.
For persistent hypercapnic failure after an admission; pCO2 is not raised enough here.
Not the next step for hypoxaemia alone.
Not recommended; no survival benefit.

steps.x: **C. Long-term oxygen therapy.** LTOT: PaO2 below 7.3, or 7.3-8 with oedema, polycythaemia or pulmonary hypertension.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man with COPD has an exacerbation. Despite 1 hour of controlled oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics, he remains breathless. He is alert. His pulse rate is 108 bpm, BP 142/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% on 28% oxygen.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: A respiratory acidosis (pH 7.25-7.35) with raised pCO2 that persists after optimal medical therapy is the indication for NIV (BiPAP).

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now.
Persistent respiratory acidosis (pH 7.25-7.35) with raised pCO2 after medical therapy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **NIV (BiPAP)**.

elim: An acute asthma treatment; does not treat ventilatory failure.
Sats are on target; more oxygen will worsen CO2.
For NIV failure or contraindication.
He is already on antibiotics; this does not treat acidosis.

steps.x: **D. Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP).** pH 7.25-7.35 + raised pCO2 after treatment = NIV.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man with severe COPD and chronic hypoxaemia develops ankle oedema and a raised JVP. Echocardiography shows a dilated, hypertrophied right ventricle and raised pulmonary artery pressure. His left ventricular function is normal. His pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 126/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his pulmonary hypertension?
o: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and vascular remodelling
practice.e: Chronic hypoxia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction and vascular remodelling, raising pulmonary pressure and causing RV hypertrophy and failure (cor pulmonale).

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to its mechanism.
Chronic hypoxia, right heart failure, normal left heart.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hypoxia constricts pulmonary arterioles and remodels them: **pulmonary hypertension**, then RV hypertrophy (cor pulmonale).

elim: Needs a history of PE; COPD with hypoxia explains it.
LV function is normal, so not post-capillary.
Congenital heart disease is not described.
Portopulmonary hypertension needs liver disease.

steps.x: **B. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and vascular remodelling.** Cor pulmonale mechanism = hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.
